goals: Reduce client-observed p99 latency (especially for GETs) at high load by minimizing time spent queued behind slow SCAN requests in per-socket UDP receive queues.
Keep all reuseport workers reasonably utilized while avoiding pathological per-worker queue build-up, even with a single client UDP flow and an open-loop sender.

Exploit the GET/SCAN service-time skew by steering SCANs away from GETs via simple, static lane partitioning using only existing maps (pebble_udp_targets, pebble_agent_state) and no extra user-space configuration.
Maintain a verifier-friendly, stateless-per-packet selector: O(1) work per packet, no per-flow state, and no new BPF maps beyond the existing pebble_agent_state.
evidence: Server perf logs with the current agent selector show even packet distribution across all 6 workers and stable in-handler latencies (avg_get ≈10–11 µs, avg_scan ≈2 ms) with zero errors, confirming that basic load-balancing and handler behavior are correct.

Client logs show sent==recv but outstanding requests and overall p99 latency rise sharply with load, reaching ~16 ms p99 at 140k req/s, indicating that delays are dominated by queueing outside the handler (kernel UDP receive queues).

With per-packet stateless random routing over 6 workers, each worker behaves as an independent M/G/1 queue. Given GET≈10 µs, SCAN≈2 ms, and SCAN fraction≈0.5%, SCANs and GETs each consume roughly half of the CPU time (0.995×1 + 0.005×200 ≈ 2), so occasional SCANs can cause large head-of-line blocking for many queued GETs on the same worker.

The client’s end-to-end measurements expose the heavy queueing tails, whereas server-side metrics measure only time inside handleRequest (post-ReadFromUDP) and therefore do not capture kernel queue delays.

Code inspection confirms that pebble_udp_targets is densely populated with worker fds at indices 0..workers-1, and pebble_agent_state.Active is set once at startup to the exact worker count, giving the selector a reliable active worker range.

cmd/workload_client always emits ASCII payloads starting with exact prefixes "GET " or "SCAN ", so the eBPF selector can reliably classify request type by inspecting only the first 4–5 bytes of the packet.
architecture: Retain a single sk_reuseport/selector program AgentUDPSelector that reads pebble_agent_state[0].Active as the active worker count (clamped to the sockarray max) and never modifies the state map, keeping the selector effectively stateless per packet.

On each packet, safely read the first few bytes from sk_reuseport_md->data/data_end and classify the request as GET if the payload begins with "GET " (0x47 0x45 0x54 0x20), as SCAN if it begins with "SCAN " (0x53 0x43 0x41 0x4e 0x20), and otherwise treat it as GET-like for routing purposes.

Deterministically partition the [0, active) worker index space into two contiguous lanes based solely on active: let scan_workers = active / 2 (integer division) and get_workers = active - scan_workers; if 0 < scan_workers < active, define SCAN lane = [get_workers, active) and GET lane = [0, get_workers), otherwise fall back to a single unified lane [0, active) with no type-based split.

For each packet, derive a mixed pseudo-random value from reuse->hash and bpf_get_prandom_u32(), optionally run through a simple linear congruential step, and choose a slot uniformly within the appropriate lane: for GET-like traffic, index = mixed % get_workers; for SCAN, index = get_workers + (mixed % scan_workers); when lanes are disabled, index = mixed % active.

Invoke bpf_sk_select_reuseport(reuse, &pebble_udp_targets, &index, 0) exactly once per packet and return SK_PASS, letting the kernel reuseport logic honor the chosen worker while preserving per-packet statelessness and even distribution within each lane.
risks: Static 50/50 lane partitioning (scan_workers = active / 2) is tuned to the observed workload where GET and SCAN consume roughly equal total CPU despite very different frequencies. If the GET/SCAN mix or relative service times change significantly (e.g., many more SCANs or much slower SCANs), this split could under- or over-provision the SCAN lane, increasing either SCAN or GET queueing.

For configurations with very few workers (e.g., active=2), an even split means only one GET worker, which can be close to saturation at high total request rates; the design optimizes mainly for the evaluated 6-worker configuration and may show higher tails at extreme loads with small worker counts.

The selector assumes all current operations are either GET or SCAN and defaults unknown prefixes into the GET lane. If new, slower operation types are introduced without updating the classifier, they may be misrouted into the GET lane and reintroduce head-of-line blocking for GETs.

The design relies on safe access to packet payload in the sk_reuseport_md context via data/data_end. While this is standard for reuseport programs, any kernel or verifier differences that restrict payload access would require simplifying the classifier or reverting to hash-only selection.

Because no per-worker queue information is available and no runtime feedback is used, the selector cannot react to transient load imbalances or hotspots within a lane; it only reduces cross-type interference by separating GET and SCAN queues, but residual tail latency from random arrival bursts within each lane will still exist.

goals: Reduce client-observed p99 latency for GET requests at high load by minimizing time spent queued behind slow SCAN requests in per-socket UDP receive queues.
Prevent pathological per-worker queue build-up while still spreading traffic across all reuseport workers, even when there is only a single client UDP flow and a purely open-loop sender.
Exploit the known GET/SCAN service-time skew by steering SCANs away from GETs (separate 'lanes') using only existing eBPF maps and without adding user-space configuration.
Keep the selector as simple and verifier-friendly as possible: stateless beyond the existing pebble_agent_state map, O(1) work per packet, no new maps, and no dependence on per-flow state.
evidence: Server perf logs show even packet distribution across all 6 workers and stable in-handler latencies (avg_get ≈10–11 µs, avg_scan ≈2 ms) with zero errors, indicating the current per-packet random selector is balancing traffic and the handlers themselves are behaving as configured.

Client logs show sent==recv but outstanding requests and overall p99 latency rise sharply with load, reaching ~16 ms p99 at 140k req/s, which implies significant queueing delay is being added outside the handler (i.e., in kernel UDP receive queues).

With one client UDP socket and stateless per-packet random routing, each worker behaves like an independent M/G/1 queue. Rare SCANs (~0.5% but ≈200× slower than GETs) occasionally occupy a worker for ~2 ms while dozens of new GETs are randomly assigned to the same worker, creating long per-socket queues and head-of-line blocking.

Because the server’s latency metrics measure only time inside handleRequest (after ReadFromUDP), they do not capture kernel queueing delays, while the client measures end-to-end latency and therefore exposes the high tail that arises from those queues.

Under these conditions, the primary performance problem is not imbalance across workers but GETs being randomly co-located with slow SCANs on the same worker socket, amplifying queueing variance and inflating GET p99 latency.
architecture: Extend the sk_reuseport/selector to minimally parse the incoming UDP payload (using sk_reuseport_md->data/data_end) and classify each request as GET-like (fast) or SCAN-like (slow) based on its ASCII prefix (e.g., leading 'G' vs 'S').

Use the existing pebble_agent_state.active to determine the current number of workers and partition the reuseport sockarray indices into two disjoint groups: a SCAN lane (roughly half of the [0, active) slots) and a GET lane (the remaining slots), with simple deterministic sizing that does not require user-space tuning.

For each packet, perform a per-packet pseudo-random selection (reuse->hash mixed with bpf_get_prandom_u32) within the appropriate lane: SCANs are routed only to SCAN-lane workers, GETs only to GET-lane workers, falling back to the full [0, active) set when there is only one worker or the partition collapses.
risks: Assumes that entries in the pebble_udp_targets BPF_MAP_TYPE_REUSEPORT_SOCKARRAY are populated densely from index 0 up to (active-1) and that these indices map 1:1 to distinct server worker goroutines; if the server uses a different indexing scheme, the lane partitioning could be ineffective or misaligned.

Assumes that all current requests are ASCII-encoded and begin with distinct textual prefixes for GET and SCAN (e.g., 'GET ' vs 'SCAN '), and that no other verbs need to be handled; misclassification could reduce the benefit of lane separation.

Statically allocating a fixed fraction of workers to the SCAN lane based solely on active (e.g., about half) implicitly bakes in assumptions about the GET/SCAN mix and relative service times; if these change significantly in other experiments, the SCAN lane may be over- or under-provisioned.

Relies on sk_reuseport programs having safe access to packet payload via data/data_end within the verifier and kernel used by this project; if the actual sk_reuseport_md layout or kernel capabilities are more limited, payload parsing might need to be adjusted or simplified.

Assumes pebble_agent_state.active is set once at startup and remains constant; if the server ever changes the active worker count at runtime, we must confirm that the selector continues to see consistent state and that the lane partitioning logic behaves sensibly.

rag_answers.question: In internal/server/ebpf.go, how is the pebble_agent_state map used for the 'agent' policy (specifically: which struct fields are written from Go, and is the Active field always set to the number of reuseport workers)?

answer.answer:
For the 'agent' policy, the Go code writes a single `ebpfutil.AgentSelectorAgentState` value into the `PebbleAgentState` map at key `uint32(0)`. The only field explicitly set from Go is `Active`:

- A local `state` variable is constructed as:
  - `state := ebpfutil.AgentSelectorAgentState{ Active: uint32(workers) }`
- This `state` is then written to the map with:
  - `objs.PebbleAgentState.Update(&key, &state, ebpf.UpdateAny)`

No other fields of `AgentSelectorAgentState` are modified in this function. As implemented, the `Active` field is always set directly from the `workers` argument (converted to `uint32`), after validating that `workers` is non‑negative. If `workers < 0`, the function returns an error and does not update the map at all.

rag_answers.question: In internal/server/ebpf.go (or related helpers), how are worker socket fds inserted into the pebble_udp_targets BPF_MAP_TYPE_REUSEPORT_SOCKARRAY — is the map key always equal to the worker index in [0, workers), with no gaps or reordering?

answer.answer:
Worker socket fds are inserted into the reuseport sockarray with the map key equal to the worker index, with no gaps or reordering.

The helper responsible for this is `updateTargetsMap(slot uint32, fd int)` in `internal/server/ebpf.go`. It takes a `slot` parameter and writes the given socket fd into the eBPF map at that exact key:

- It opens the pinned map (the `pebble_udp_targets` sockarray) via `ebpf.LoadPinnedMap(targetMapPath(), nil)`.
- It converts the fd to `uint32` and calls `m.Update(&slot, &value, ebpf.UpdateAny)` — so the key in the map is exactly the `slot` argument provided by the caller.

Separately, `clearTargets(numSlots int)` iterates keys from `0` up to `numSlots-1` and deletes each key, which also assumes a dense, zero-based index space for the map keys.

Given these implementations, the intended usage is that each worker’s socket fd is stored at the index corresponding to its worker index in the range `[0, workers)`, with no gaps or reordering.

rag_answers.question: What is the exact on-the-wire format produced by cmd/workload_client for GET and SCAN requests (e.g., precise ASCII prefixes, capitalization, and spacing) in buildPayload, so the eBPF program can classify them reliably using only the first few bytes?

answer.answer:
cmd/workload_client sends ASCII UDP payloads with this exact format:

- General pattern (both GET and SCAN):
  "<REQTYPE><space><KEY><space><REQID>"

  where `<space>` is the single ASCII space character `' '` (0x20), and there are no leading or trailing spaces beyond those shown.

- For GET requests:
  1. The payload starts with the uppercase letters:
     "GET" (bytes: 0x47 0x45 0x54)
  2. Followed by exactly one space character (0x20).
  3. Then the key string `<KEY>` (see key format below).
  4. Then exactly one space character (0x20).
  5. Then the request ID `<REQID>` as ASCII hex plus a 1-byte type suffix (see below for details).

  So the beginning of every GET request is exactly:
  "GET "

- For SCAN requests:
  1. The payload starts with the uppercase letters:
     "SCAN" (bytes: 0x53 0x43 0x41 0x4e)
  2. Followed by exactly one space character (0x20).
  3. Then the key string `<KEY>` (see key format below).
  4. Then exactly one space character (0x20).
  5. Then the decimal scan limit `<SCANLIMIT>` in ASCII digits (no leading spaces, no sign).
  6. Then exactly one space character (0x20).
  7. Then the request ID `<REQID>` as ASCII hex plus a 1-byte type suffix.

  So the beginning of every SCAN request is exactly:
  "SCAN "

- KEY format (`appendKey`):
  * The key always starts with the configured prefix string `prefix` exactly as given (case-sensitive, no added delimiters).
  * After `prefix`, a numeric key index is appended:
    - If `keyIdx < 100000000` (i.e., 0–99,999,999), it is encoded as an 8-digit, zero-padded decimal number, e.g., 0 → "00000000", 42 → "00000042".
    - If `keyIdx >= 100000000`, it is encoded as a decimal integer with no padding.

  So `<KEY>` is:
  "<prefix><8-digit-zero-padded-decimal>" (for small indices) or
  "<prefix><decimal-without-padding>" (for large indices).

- REQID format (`makeReqID`):
  * `<REQID>` is a fixed-length ASCII string of length `idTotalLen`.
  * It consists of:
    1. A hex-encoded send timestamp in nanoseconds (`sendNano`), occupying `idTimeHexLen` characters, using lowercase hex digits from the constant `hexDigits`.
    2. Immediately followed by a hex-encoded sequence number (`seq`), occupying `idSeqHexLen` characters, also lowercase hex.
    3. A final single-byte type marker at the very end (position `idTotalLen-1`):
       - For GET: the last byte is `reqTypeGet`.
       - For SCAN: the last byte is `reqTypeScan`.
  * All hex characters are contiguous, with no spaces or delimiters between time and sequence portions.

- Summary for eBPF classification using only initial bytes:
  * GET requests always begin with:
    "GET "
    i.e., bytes [0..3] = 0x47 0x45 0x54 0x20.
  * SCAN requests always begin with:
    "SCAN "
    i.e., bytes [0..4] = 0x53 0x43 0x41 0x4e 0x20.
  * All subsequent delimiters between components (`KEY`, optional `SCANLIMIT`, `REQID`) are single ASCII spaces.

rag_answers.question: Does the current ebpf/agentselector.c source in the repo match the 'best program' snippet provided (in terms of map definitions and the struct agent_state layout), or have there been additional fields or maps introduced that the new design must preserve?

answer.answer:
The current eBPF agent selector used by the server is represented on the Go side by the `ebpfutil.AgentSelectorObjects` type and its related maps and structs.

From the server’s interaction with these objects:
- There is a map `PebbleAgentState` that stores values of type `ebpfutil.AgentSelectorAgentState`.
- The `AgentSelectorAgentState` struct is expected to have at least one field:
  - `Active uint32` – this is what the server populates from the `workers` parameter.
- The map key for `PebbleAgentState` is a `uint32` (the code always uses key `0`).

No additional fields in `AgentSelectorAgentState` are referenced by the server code, and no additional maps related to agent state or target selection are manipulated beyond:
- `PebbleAgentState` (agent state map), and
- `pebble_udp_targets` (the pinned target map used by `updateTargetsMap` and `clearTargets`).

`updateTargetsMap` and `clearTargets` operate only on a single pinned map located at `pinDirectory()/"pebble_udp_targets"`, with keys and values both being `uint32`. There are no extra maps referenced that the new design must carry forward.

Therefore, for the purposes of compatibility with the current server implementation, the important requirements the new design must preserve are:
1. A pinned map for agent state (named and wired so that it is exposed as `PebbleAgentState` in `AgentSelectorObjects`), with key type `uint32` and value type `struct agent_state` whose first (and required) field is a `uint32` count of active workers.
2. A pinned map named `pebble_udp_targets` with `uint32` keys (slots) and `uint32` values (file descriptors or similar identifiers).

If the original “best program” snippet defined only these two maps and had an `agent_state` struct whose layout corresponds to a single `uint32 Active` field at the start, then it still matches the server’s expectations. If that snippet omitted any of the above, or changed key/value types, then the current implementation has introduced requirements (the `Active` field and these two pinned maps) that the new design must preserve.

rag_answers.question: Besides agentselector.c, what other sk_reuseport selector programs exist under the ebpf/ directory (e.g., hash-based or scan_split variants), and do any of them already perform request-type-aware routing that could inform the GET/SCAN lane partitioning design?

answer.answer:
Under the eBPF loading logic, three distinct sk_reuseport selector programs are supported, each with its own object set:

1. A hash‑based selector (named "hash")
   - Loaded via `loadHash` using `ebpfutil.HashSelectorObjects`.
   - Uses the `HashUdpSelector` program attached as the sk_reuseport selector.
   - Maintains a `PebbleHashState` map with a `HashSelectorHashState{ Active: uint32(workers) }`, which only tracks the number of active workers.
   - Validates `workers >= 0` but has no additional routing logic exposed here.

2. A round‑robin selector (named "round_robin")
   - Loaded via `loadRoundRobin` using `ebpfutil.RrSelectorObjects`.
   - Uses the `RrUdpSelector` program as the sk_reuseport selector.
   - Maintains a `PebbleRrState` map storing `RrSelectorRrState{ Active, Counter }`:
     - On first lookup failure, initializes `Active = workers` and `Counter = 0`.
     - On subsequent loads, updates `Active` while preserving `Counter`.
   - This implements a pure round‑robin policy driven by a counter and the active worker count.

3. A scan_split selector (named "scan_split")
   - Loaded via `loadScanSplit` using `ebpfutil.ScanSplitSelectorObjects`.
   - Uses the `SplitUdpSelector` program as the sk_reuseport selector.
   - Maintains a `PebbleSplitState` map with `ScanSplitSelectorSplitState{ Active: uint32(workers) }`, again just tracking the number of active workers.
   - Also validates that `workers` is non‑negative.

All three selectors expose only a simple control surface from user space: the number of active workers (and, for round robin, an internal counter). None of these loaders configure any per‑request fields, request types, or key ranges, nor do they differentiate GET vs SCAN or any other operation types at this layer. They are generic load‑balancing primitives (hash, round‑robin, and a split policy that is parameterized only by an "Active" count), not request‑type‑aware routers.

So, beyond the existing agentselector.c‑style selector, there are hash, round‑robin, and scan_split selector programs under the eBPF directory, but they do not currently implement request‑type‑aware routing that would directly drive a GET/SCAN lane partitioning design. They may serve as structural patterns (e.g., map‑based state, pinning, reuseport attach), but new logic would be required to route based on request type.

goals: Reduce client-observed p99 latency (especially for GETs) at high load by minimizing time spent queued behind slow SCAN requests in per-socket UDP receive queues.
Keep all reuseport workers reasonably utilized while avoiding pathological per-worker queue build-up, even with a single client UDP flow and an open-loop sender.

Exploit the GET/SCAN service-time skew by steering SCANs away from GETs via simple, static lane partitioning using only existing maps (pebble_udp_targets, pebble_agent_state) and no extra user-space configuration.
Maintain a verifier-friendly, stateless-per-packet selector: O(1) work per packet, no per-flow state, and no new BPF maps beyond the existing pebble_agent_state.
evidence: Server perf logs with the current agent selector show even packet distribution across all 6 workers and stable in-handler latencies (avg_get ≈10–11 µs, avg_scan ≈2 ms) with zero errors, confirming that basic load-balancing and handler behavior are correct.

Client logs show sent==recv but outstanding requests and overall p99 latency rise sharply with load, reaching ~16 ms p99 at 140k req/s, indicating that delays are dominated by queueing outside the handler (kernel UDP receive queues).

With per-packet stateless random routing over 6 workers, each worker behaves as an independent M/G/1 queue. Given GET≈10 µs, SCAN≈2 ms, and SCAN fraction≈0.5%, SCANs and GETs each consume roughly half of the CPU time (0.995×1 + 0.005×200 ≈ 2), so occasional SCANs can cause large head-of-line blocking for many queued GETs on the same worker.

The client’s end-to-end measurements expose the heavy queueing tails, whereas server-side metrics measure only time inside handleRequest (post-ReadFromUDP) and therefore do not capture kernel queue delays.

Code inspection confirms that pebble_udp_targets is densely populated with worker fds at indices 0..workers-1, and pebble_agent_state.Active is set once at startup to the exact worker count, giving the selector a reliable active worker range.

cmd/workload_client always emits ASCII payloads starting with exact prefixes "GET " or "SCAN ", so the eBPF selector can reliably classify request type by inspecting only the first 4–5 bytes of the packet.
architecture: Retain a single sk_reuseport/selector program AgentUDPSelector that reads pebble_agent_state[0].Active as the active worker count (clamped to the sockarray max) and never modifies the state map, keeping the selector effectively stateless per packet.

On each packet, safely read the first few bytes from sk_reuseport_md->data/data_end and classify the request as GET if the payload begins with "GET " (0x47 0x45 0x54 0x20), as SCAN if it begins with "SCAN " (0x53 0x43 0x41 0x4e 0x20), and otherwise treat it as GET-like for routing purposes.

Deterministically partition the [0, active) worker index space into two contiguous lanes based solely on active: let scan_workers = active / 2 (integer division) and get_workers = active - scan_workers; if 0 < scan_workers < active, define SCAN lane = [get_workers, active) and GET lane = [0, get_workers), otherwise fall back to a single unified lane [0, active) with no type-based split.

For each packet, derive a mixed pseudo-random value from reuse->hash and bpf_get_prandom_u32(), optionally run through a simple linear congruential step, and choose a slot uniformly within the appropriate lane: for GET-like traffic, index = mixed % get_workers; for SCAN, index = get_workers + (mixed % scan_workers); when lanes are disabled, index = mixed % active.

Invoke bpf_sk_select_reuseport(reuse, &pebble_udp_targets, &index, 0) exactly once per packet and return SK_PASS, letting the kernel reuseport logic honor the chosen worker while preserving per-packet statelessness and even distribution within each lane.
risks: Static 50/50 lane partitioning (scan_workers = active / 2) is tuned to the observed workload where GET and SCAN consume roughly equal total CPU despite very different frequencies. If the GET/SCAN mix or relative service times change significantly (e.g., many more SCANs or much slower SCANs), this split could under- or over-provision the SCAN lane, increasing either SCAN or GET queueing.

For configurations with very few workers (e.g., active=2), an even split means only one GET worker, which can be close to saturation at high total request rates; the design optimizes mainly for the evaluated 6-worker configuration and may show higher tails at extreme loads with small worker counts.

The selector assumes all current operations are either GET or SCAN and defaults unknown prefixes into the GET lane. If new, slower operation types are introduced without updating the classifier, they may be misrouted into the GET lane and reintroduce head-of-line blocking for GETs.

The design relies on safe access to packet payload in the sk_reuseport_md context via data/data_end. While this is standard for reuseport programs, any kernel or verifier differences that restrict payload access would require simplifying the classifier or reverting to hash-only selection.

Because no per-worker queue information is available and no runtime feedback is used, the selector cannot react to transient load imbalances or hotspots within a lane; it only reduces cross-type interference by separating GET and SCAN queues, but residual tail latency from random arrival bursts within each lane will still exist.
